claim: Pain is heavily modulated by expectations.
source: Pain is heavily modulated by expectations.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus in the pain research field.

claim: Positive expectations can lead to hypoalgesia (placebo effect).
source: Positive expectations can lead to hypoalgesia (placebo effect), while negative expectations can increase the perceived intensity of pain (nocebo effect; Kong and Benedetti, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kong and Benedetti, 2014.

claim: Negative expectations can increase the perceived intensity of pain (nocebo effect).
source: Positive expectations can lead to hypoalgesia (placebo effect), while negative expectations can increase the perceived intensity of pain (nocebo effect; Kong and Benedetti, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kong and Benedetti, 2014.

claim: The neuronal processes underlying the generation of expectations prior to the appearance of the pain stimulus are not yet fully understood.
source: Although many studies have shown that expectations can influence pain perception, the neuronal processes underlying the generation of expectations prior to the appearance of the pain stimulus are not yet fully understood (Benedetti, 2014; Büchel et al., 2014; Koyama et al., 2005; Wager and Atlas, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations indicating gaps in current knowledge.

claim: Placebo and nocebo effects influence brain activity during pain perception.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that placebo and nocebo effects influence brain activity during pain perception (Egorova et al., 2015; Wager and Atlas, 2015; Zunhammer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The descending pain modulatory system (DPMS) is associated with placebo and nocebo effects.
source: Especially the descending pain modulatory system (DPMS; Geuter et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2022) is associated with placebo and nocebo effects and is thought to consist of areas like the periaqueductal gray (PAG), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and amygdala (Eippert et al., 2009), as well as frontal areas like the vmPFC (Geuter et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing the DPMS and its components.

claim: The DPMS consists of areas like the periaqueductal gray (PAG), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and amygdala.
source: Especially the descending pain modulatory system (DPMS; Geuter et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2022) is associated with placebo and nocebo effects and is thought to consist of areas like the periaqueductal gray (PAG), dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), and amygdala (Eippert et al., 2009), as well as frontal areas like the vmPFC (Geuter et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing the DPMS components.

claim: Placebo and nocebo effects modulate activity in areas classically associated with pain processing like the thalamus and the insula during noxious stimulation.
source: Furthermore, placebo and nocebo effects modulate activity in areas classically associated with pain processing like the thalamus and the insula during noxious stimulation (Atlas and Wager, 2014; Wager and Atlas, 2015; Wager et al., 2004; Zunhammer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies showing modulation of pain-related brain areas.

claim: Expectations are generated prior to the appearance of the stimulus and should be reflected in anticipatory neural activity.
source: A central feature of expectations is that they are generated prior to the appearance of the stimulus and should, therefore, be reflected in anticipatory neural activity (Kong et al., 2007; Wager et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations and logical inference about the temporal nature of expectations.

claim: The mere expectation of the appearance of a painful stimulus activates regions relevant to subsequent pain processing, such as the insula, DLPFC, and thalamus.
source: The mere expectation of the appearance of a painful stimulus has been shown to activate regions relevant to subsequent pain processing, such as the insula, DLPFC, and thalamus (Palermo et al., 2015; Ploghaus et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies showing anticipatory brain activation.

claim: Expecting reduced pain modulates activity in parts of the DPMS and the insula during pain anticipation.
source: Similarly, there is evidence that expecting reduced pain (e.g. via a placebo) modulates activity in parts of the DPMS and the insula already during pain anticipation (Wager et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wager et al., 2011.

claim: Placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia can be attributed to predictive coding.
source: This framework posits that placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia can be attributed to predictive coding, suggesting that perception is the result of a constant matching of incoming sensory data with the top-down predictions of an internal or generative model (Büchel et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Büchel et al., 2014 describing the predictive coding framework.

claim: The neural mechanisms of expectation generation before the stimulus remain unclear.
source: However, the neural mechanisms of this process remain unclear, with little information about where and how the expectations relevant to these top-down predictions are generated.
evidence: Statement about gaps in current knowledge.

claim: It is uncertain whether the anticipatory modulation reflects only a pre-activation of later relevant networks or indicates functionally distinct processes in expectation generation.
source: Furthermore, it is uncertain whether the anticipatory modulation reported in the literature reflects only a pre-activation of later relevant networks or indicates functionally distinct processes in expectation generation.
evidence: Statement about uncertainty in the field based on existing literature.

claim: Positive and negative expectations show varying correlations with the amount of prior experience and differences in learning.
source: On the basis of behavioral differences between positive and negative expectations, such as their varying correlations with the amount of prior experience and differences in learning (Colloca et al., 2010; Colloca et al., 2008), it seems reasonable to assume at least partially dissimilar neural representations of positive and negative expectations.
evidence: Supported by citations to Colloca et al. studies.

claim: There is evidence of distinct neural processes for positive and negative expectations during pain perception.
source: Especially during pain perception, there is evidence of distinct neural processes for positive and negative expectations, as well as valence-dependent modulation of similar systems.
evidence: General statement about existing evidence in the literature.

claim: Some findings suggest differential modulation of activity in key areas of the DPMS and reward system by the valence of expectations.
source: More specifically, some findings suggest differential modulation of activity in key areas of the DPMS and reward system by the valence of expectations (Benedetti et al., 2020; Crawford et al., 2021; Koyama et al., 2005; Scott et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Some studies have reported the absence of shared brain activations during the perception of pain for positive and negative expectations.
source: Alternatively, some studies have reported the absence of shared brain activations during the perception of pain (Bingel et al., 2011; Freeman et al., 2015; Fu et al., 2021; Shi et al., 2021; Shih et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Some areas have been reported to be specifically activated for either placebo or nocebo during pain anticipation.
source: Similar findings have been reported during pain anticipation, as some areas have been reported to be specifically activated for either placebo or nocebo (Fu et al., 2021; Rossettini et al., 2023) or show opposing valence-dependent responses (Amanzio et al., 2013; Kong et al., 2008; Palermo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies.

claim: There is conflicting evidence of shared anticipatory activation for both placebo and nocebo in some areas of the DPMS like the DLPFC and ACC.
source: However, there is conflicting evidence of shared anticipatory activation for both placebo and nocebo in some areas of the DPMS like the DLPFC and ACC (Amanzio et al., 2013; Amanzio and Palermo, 2019; Colloca and Benedetti, 2007; Frisaldi et al., 2015; Manaï et al., 2019; Palermo et al., 2015; Rossettini et al., 2023; Schmid et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing conflicting results.

claim: The insula is recognized for its function as a multimodal network hub.
source: A potential candidate for this integration process is the insula, which is recognized for its function as a multimodal network hub (Adler-Neal et al., 2019; Dionisio et al., 2019; Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies describing the insula's function.

claim: The insula is associated with threat in fear conditioning.
source: The multimodal role of the insula is further reflected in its role in fear conditioning, with the insula being associated with threat (Fullana et al., 2016), while other areas that are important for placebo modulations like the vmPFC are closely connected to the default mode network, potentially reflecting a safety signal (Fullana et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fullana et al., 2016.

claim: The vmPFC is closely connected to the default mode network, potentially reflecting a safety signal.
source: The multimodal role of the insula is further reflected in its role in fear conditioning, with the insula being associated with threat (Fullana et al., 2016), while other areas that are important for placebo modulations like the vmPFC are closely connected to the default mode network, potentially reflecting a safety signal (Fullana et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fullana et al., 2016 and involves speculative interpretation.

claim: Prefrontal areas have been suggested to provide predictions for downstream pain-sensitive systems.
source: Within the DPMS, prefrontal areas have been suggested to provide predictions for downstream pain-sensitive systems, implying an early role within this system (Geuter et al., 2017; Koban et al., 2017; Wager and Atlas, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies.

claim: The study investigated 50 participants (32 female) in a combined EEG-fMRI paradigm.
source: In total, we investigated 50 participants (32 female) in a combined EEG-fMRI paradigm.
evidence: Direct statement about the study sample.

claim: Participants were told that they would be given real-time visual feedback on their current pain sensitivity based on their EEG activity using a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI).
source: In short, participants were told that they would be given real-time visual feedback on their current pain sensitivity based on their EEG activity using a Brain-Computer Interface (BCI).
evidence: Description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The visual cues were not related to any brain activity but were only used to produce the corresponding expectations.
source: In fact, the visual cues were not related to any brain activity but were only used to produce the corresponding expectations.
evidence: Description of the experimental deception.

claim: Red cues were paired with higher pain intensity (VAS level 70) during the learning phase.
source: Here, red cues were paired with higher pain intensity (VAS level 70), while green cues were paired with lower pain intensity (VAS level 30).
evidence: Description of the conditioning procedure.

claim: Green cues were paired with lower pain intensity (VAS level 30) during the learning phase.
source: Here, red cues were paired with higher pain intensity (VAS level 70), while green cues were paired with lower pain intensity (VAS level 30).
evidence: Description of the conditioning procedure.

claim: In the test phase, temperatures were kept constant (VAS level 60).
source: In the ensuing test phase (see Figure 1), temperatures were kept constant (VAS level 60).
evidence: Description of the test phase procedure.

claim: Participants were unaware that the stimulation temperature was always exactly the same in the test phase.
source: Participants were informed that they would receive different pain stimuli of medium intensity and were unaware that the stimulation temperature was always exactly the same.
evidence: Description of the experimental deception.

claim: There was a significant main effect of condition on mean expectation ratings (F(2,98) = 86.51, p<0.001, ηP²=0.64).
source: Our data showed successfully induced expectations in line with the cued sham brain states as evidenced by a significant main effect of condition in a repeated-measures ANOVA for mean expectation ratings (F(2,98) = 86.51, p<0.001, ηP²=0.64; see Figure 2A).
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data, also shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Expectation ratings were higher in the nocebo (M=65.80, SD = 15.80) compared to the control condition (M=48.58, SD = 13.79, p<0.001).
source: Expectation ratings were higher in the nocebo (M=65.80, SD = 15.80) compared to the control condition (M=48.58, SD = 13.79, p<0.001), which in turn were higher than in the placebo condition (M=34.33, SD=17.71, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: Expectation ratings in the control condition were higher than in the placebo condition (M=34.33, SD=17.71, p<0.001).
source: Expectation ratings were higher in the nocebo (M=65.80, SD = 15.80) compared to the control condition (M=48.58, SD = 13.79, p<0.001), which in turn were higher than in the placebo condition (M=34.33, SD=17.71, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: Mean pain ratings were affected by the experimental manipulation (rmANOVA: F(2,98) = 63.00, p<0.001, ηP²=0.56).
source: Similarly, mean pain ratings were affected by our manipulation (rmANOVA: F(2,98) = 63.00, p<0.001, ηP²=0.56; see Figure 2B).
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data, also shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pain ratings were higher in the nocebo (M=56.80, SD=14.21) compared to the control condition (M=51.40, SD=14.31, p<0.001).
source: Post-hoc Tukey tests revealed higher pain ratings in the nocebo (M=56.80, SD=14.21) compared to the control condition (M=51.40, SD=14.31, p<0.001), which in turn led to higher pain ratings than the placebo condition (M=44.88, SD=15.06, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: Pain ratings in the control condition were higher than in the placebo condition (M=44.88, SD=15.06, p<0.001).
source: Post-hoc Tukey tests revealed higher pain ratings in the nocebo (M=56.80, SD=14.21) compared to the control condition (M=51.40, SD=14.31, p<0.001), which in turn led to higher pain ratings than the placebo condition (M=44.88, SD=15.06, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: Placebo and nocebo effects were significantly correlated across subjects for expectation ratings (r=0.64, p<0.001).
source: Moreover, placebo (control - placebo) and nocebo (nocebo - control) effects were significantly correlated across subjects for both expectation (r=0.64, p<0.001) and pain ratings (r=0.30, p=0.033), indicating that subjects who experienced stronger placebo effects also experienced larger nocebo effects.
evidence: Correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: Placebo and nocebo effects were significantly correlated across subjects for pain ratings (r=0.30, p=0.033).
source: Moreover, placebo (control - placebo) and nocebo (nocebo - control) effects were significantly correlated across subjects for both expectation (r=0.64, p<0.001) and pain ratings (r=0.30, p=0.033), indicating that subjects who experienced stronger placebo effects also experienced larger nocebo effects.
evidence: Correlation analysis from the study data.

claim: Subjects who experienced stronger placebo effects also experienced larger nocebo effects.
source: Moreover, placebo (control - placebo) and nocebo (nocebo - control) effects were significantly correlated across subjects for both expectation (r=0.64, p<0.001) and pain ratings (r=0.30, p=0.033), indicating that subjects who experienced stronger placebo effects also experienced larger nocebo effects.
evidence: Interpretation of correlation results from the study data.

claim: There were differences in relative variance indices between conditions for expectation ratings (F(2,96) = 8.14, p<0.001).
source: We observed differences in relative variance indices between conditions for both expectation (F(2,96) = 8.14, p<0.001) and pain ratings (F(2,96) = 3.41, p=0.037).
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data.

claim: There were differences in relative variance indices between conditions for pain ratings (F(2,96) = 3.41, p=0.037).
source: We observed differences in relative variance indices between conditions for both expectation (F(2,96) = 8.14, p<0.001) and pain ratings (F(2,96) = 3.41, p=0.037).
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data.

claim: There was significantly more variance in the placebo compared to the control condition for both expectation and pain ratings.
source: For both measures, post-hoc tests revealed that there was significantly more variance in the placebo compared to the control condition (both pholm<0.05), but no difference between control and nocebo.
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: Variance in expectation ratings decreased from the first block compared to the other two blocks (F(1.35,64.64)=5.69, p=0.012).
source: Variance in expectation ratings decreased from the first block compared to the other two blocks (F(1.35,64.64)=5.69, p=0.012; both pholm<0.05), which was not the case for pain ratings.
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data.

claim: There was no interaction effect of block and condition for expectation ratings (F(2.65,127.06)=0.40, p=0.728).
source: There was no interaction effect of block and condition for neither expectation (F(2.65,127.06)=0.40, p=0.728) nor pain ratings (F(4,192) = 0.48, p=0.748), which implies that expectations were similarly dynamically updated in all conditions over the course of the experiment.
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data.

claim: There was no interaction effect of block and condition for pain ratings (F(4,192) = 0.48, p=0.748).
source: There was no interaction effect of block and condition for neither expectation (F(2.65,127.06)=0.40, p=0.728) nor pain ratings (F(4,192) = 0.48, p=0.748), which implies that expectations were similarly dynamically updated in all conditions over the course of the experiment.
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data.

claim: Expectations were similarly dynamically updated in all conditions over the course of the experiment.
source: There was no interaction effect of block and condition for neither expectation (F(2.65,127.06)=0.40, p=0.728) nor pain ratings (F(4,192) = 0.48, p=0.748), which implies that expectations were similarly dynamically updated in all conditions over the course of the experiment.
evidence: Inference drawn from the statistical results.

claim: The expectation manipulation affected skin conductance responses (SCRs) to the pain stimuli (rmANOVA: F(2,50) = 4.33, p=0.018, ηP²=0.15).
source: The expectation manipulation not only affected behavioral ratings but also the skin conductance responses (SCRs) to the pain stimuli (rmANOVA: F(2,50) = 4.33, p=0.018, ηP²=0.15; see Figure 2C).
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data, also shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SCRs were larger in the nocebo (M=0.05, SD=0.09) compared to the placebo condition (M=–0.04, SD=0.10, p=0.049).
source: A post-hoc Tukey test showed larger SCRs in the nocebo (M=0.05, SD=0.09) compared to the placebo condition (M=–0.04, SD=0.10, p=0.049).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: SCRs in the control condition (M=–0.01, SD=0.07) did not significantly differ from the nocebo condition (p=0.072).
source: SCRs in the control condition (M=–0.01, SD=0.07) did not significantly differ from neither the nocebo (p=0.072) nor placebo condition (p=0.607).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: SCRs in the control condition did not significantly differ from the placebo condition (p=0.607).
source: SCRs in the control condition (M=–0.01, SD=0.07) did not significantly differ from neither the nocebo (p=0.072) nor placebo condition (p=0.607).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: The SIIPS has been introduced as a marker for subjective pain perception going beyond intensity differences.
source: The stimulus intensity independent pain signature (SIIPS) has been introduced as a marker for subjective pain perception going beyond intensity differences as it has been reported to be affected by psychological factors such as expectations (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2023; Woo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations describing the SIIPS.

claim: The SIIPS is affected by psychological factors such as expectations.
source: The stimulus intensity independent pain signature (SIIPS) has been introduced as a marker for subjective pain perception going beyond intensity differences as it has been reported to be affected by psychological factors such as expectations (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2023; Woo et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: There were significant differences in SIIPS scores between the three conditions within the pain period (F(2,88) = 11.59, p<0.001, ηP²=0.21).
source: A rmANOVA revealed significant differences between the three conditions within the pain period (F(2,88) = 11.59, p<0.001, ηP²=0.21), with Bonferroni-corrected paired t-tests showing significant differences between the placebo and nocebo condition (t(44) = 4.79, p<0.001) and between the nocebo condition and the control condition (t(44) = 3.36, p=0.002) but not between the control and the placebo condition (t(44) = 1.35, p=0.184, see Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data, also shown in Figure 3.

claim: SIIPS scores showed significant differences between the placebo and nocebo condition (t(44) = 4.79, p<0.001).
source: A rmANOVA revealed significant differences between the three conditions within the pain period (F(2,88) = 11.59, p<0.001, ηP²=0.21), with Bonferroni-corrected paired t-tests showing significant differences between the placebo and nocebo condition (t(44) = 4.79, p<0.001) and between the nocebo condition and the control condition (t(44) = 3.36, p=0.002) but not between the control and the placebo condition (t(44) = 1.35, p=0.184, see Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: SIIPS scores showed significant differences between the nocebo condition and the control condition (t(44) = 3.36, p=0.002).
source: A rmANOVA revealed significant differences between the three conditions within the pain period (F(2,88) = 11.59, p<0.001, ηP²=0.21), with Bonferroni-corrected paired t-tests showing significant differences between the placebo and nocebo condition (t(44) = 4.79, p<0.001) and between the nocebo condition and the control condition (t(44) = 3.36, p=0.002) but not between the control and the placebo condition (t(44) = 1.35, p=0.184, see Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: SIIPS scores showed no significant difference between the control and the placebo condition (t(44) = 1.35, p=0.184).
source: A rmANOVA revealed significant differences between the three conditions within the pain period (F(2,88) = 11.59, p<0.001, ηP²=0.21), with Bonferroni-corrected paired t-tests showing significant differences between the placebo and nocebo condition (t(44) = 4.79, p<0.001) and between the nocebo condition and the control condition (t(44) = 3.36, p=0.002) but not between the control and the placebo condition (t(44) = 1.35, p=0.184, see Figure 3).
evidence: Statistical comparison from the study data.

claim: The manipulation of expectations led to significant perceptual differences.
source: We therefore conclude that the manipulation of expectations led to significant perceptual differences.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the SIIPS analysis results.

claim: The SIIPS signature failed to discern between conditions during the anticipation period (F(2,88) = 0.79, p=0.455, ηP²=0.02).
source: Contrastingly, the SIIPS signature failed to discern between conditions during the anticipation period, suggesting fundamentally distinct processes in the two phases (F(2,88) = 0.79, p=0.455, ηP²=0.02).
evidence: Statistical test result from the study data.

claim: The failure of SIIPS to discern between conditions during anticipation suggests fundamentally distinct processes in the anticipation and pain phases.
source: Contrastingly, the SIIPS signature failed to discern between conditions during the anticipation period, suggesting fundamentally distinct processes in the two phases (F(2,88) = 0.79, p=0.455, ηP²=0.02).
evidence: Inference drawn from the statistical results.

claim: There was a clear dissociation between the anticipation and pain phases with a predominantly common representation of positive and negative expectations during the anticipation phase and a later shift towards distinct effects during the pain phase.
source: In our main analysis, we found a clear dissociation between the anticipation and pain phases with a predominantly common representation of positive and negative expectations during the anticipation phase and a later shift towards distinct effects during the pain phase (see Figure 4A).
evidence: Main finding from fMRI analysis, shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Common effects of directed expectations during the anticipation phase were found in the bilateral DLPFC, bilateral ACC, and right vmPFC.
source: During the anticipation phase, common effects of directed expectations were found in several important areas of the DPMS, e.g., in the bilateral DLPFC, bilateral ACC, and right vmPFC, indicating that directed expectations were represented in a rather general and nonspecific way during this period.
evidence: Results from fMRI analysis.

claim: Directed expectations were represented in a rather general and nonspecific way during the anticipation period.
source: During the anticipation phase, common effects of directed expectations were found in several important areas of the DPMS, e.g., in the bilateral DLPFC, bilateral ACC, and right vmPFC, indicating that directed expectations were represented in a rather general and nonspecific way during this period.
evidence: Interpretation of fMRI results.

claim: With the stimulus onset, activity in DPMS areas showed differential activation between positive and negative expectations.
source: With the stimulus onset, activity in these areas showed differential activation between positive and negative expectations.
evidence: Results from fMRI analysis.

claim: Differential activity between positive and negative expectations was observed in the left insula, amygdala, thalamus, and hippocampus during the pain phase.
source: Further differential activity was observed in e.g., the left insula, amygdala, thalamus, and hippocampus during the pain phase.
evidence: Results from fMRI analysis.

claim: The bilateral DLPFC, right vmPFC, left anterior insula, and thalamus were engaged during both the anticipation and pain phases.
source: Crucially, the bilateral DLPFC, right vmPFC, left anterior insula, and thalamus were engaged during both the anticipation and pain phases (see Figure 4B).
evidence: Results from fMRI analysis, shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the bilateral DLPFC, right vmPFC, and left anterior insula, directed expectations shifted from a common towards a distinct representation (positive > negative) over time.
source: In all these areas, directed expectations shifted from a common (positive and negative > control) towards a distinct representation (positive > negative: bilateral DLPFC, right vmPFC, and left anterior insula; negative > positive: thalamus) over time.
evidence: Results from fMRI analysis.

claim: In the thalamus, directed expectations shifted from a common towards a distinct representation (negative > positive) over time.
source: In all these areas, directed expectations shifted from a common (positive and negative > control) towards a distinct representation (positive > negative: bilateral DLPFC, right vmPFC, and left anterior insula; negative > positive: thalamus) over time.
evidence: Results from fMRI analysis.

claim: The right angular gyrus was engaged throughout the time course, initially showing a common representation of positive and negative expectations during the anticipation phase and differentiating only during pain perception.
source: In addition to these areas that are frequently related to expectation effects, the right angular gyrus was also engaged throughout the time course, similarly initially showing a common representation of positive and negative expectations during the anticipation phase and differentiating only during pain perception (p<0.05 whole-brain FWE-corrected; see Figure 5).
evidence: Results from fMRI analysis, shown in Figure 5.

claim: Specific expectations were mediated by different processes during the anticipation and pain phases.
source: The differences between the anticipation and the pain phase demonstrate that specific expectations were mediated by different processes during these phases and arise from a dynamic interplay of brain regions such as the DLPFC, vmPFC, anterior insula, and thalamus over time.
evidence: Interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: Specific expectations arise from a dynamic interplay of brain regions such as the DLPFC, vmPFC, anterior insula, and thalamus over time.
source: The differences between the anticipation and the pain phase demonstrate that specific expectations were mediated by different processes during these phases and arise from a dynamic interplay of brain regions such as the DLPFC, vmPFC, anterior insula, and thalamus over time.
evidence: Interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: The earliest correlation of fMRI activity with EEG oscillatory power was found in the left DLPFC during the expectation rating at theta to low gamma frequencies in a negative direction (–6.3 until –4.4 s, 4–45.28 Hz; p=0.007).
source: The earliest correlation of fMRI activity with EEG oscillatory power was found in the left DLPFC already during the expectation rating at theta to low gamma frequencies in a negative direction (–6.3 until –4.4 s, 4–45.28 Hz; p=0.007; see Figure 6A; additional information for all regions can be found in Supplementary file 1e).
evidence: Results from combined EEG-fMRI analysis, shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Anticipatory activity in the left anterior insula was associated with decreased EEG oscillatory power during the late expectation rating and anticipation phase (−4.4 to –2.5 s) spanning from theta to low gamma frequencies (5.67–32 Hz; p<0.001).
source: Next, anticipatory activity in the left anterior insula was associated with decreased EEG oscillatory power during the late expectation rating and anticipation phase (−4.4 to –2.5 s) spanning from theta to low gamma frequencies (5.67–32 Hz; p<0.001; see Figure 6B).
evidence: Results from combined EEG-fMRI analysis, shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was a significant positive association of EEG activity with fMRI activity in the right ACC during the anticipation and early pain phase in the gamma frequency range (−3 to 0.3 s, 26.89–128 Hz; p=0.003).
source: Lastly, we found a significant positive association of EEG activity with fMRI activity in the right ACC during the anticipation and early pain phase in the gamma frequency range (−3 to 0.3 s, 26.89–128 Hz; p=0.003; see Figure 6C).
evidence: Results from combined EEG-fMRI analysis, shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Activity in the left ACC was positively correlated with EEG activity in the anticipation and pain phase (cluster 1: –2.3 to –1.3 s, 32–128 Hz; p=0.019; cluster 2: –0.9 to 0.3 s, 32–128 Hz; p=0.021).
source: As expected due to the close spatial proximity, activity in the left ACC was similarly positively correlated with EEG activity in the anticipation and pain phase (cluster 1: –2.3 to –1.3 s, 32–128 Hz; p=0.019; cluster 2: –0.9 to 0.3 s, 32–128 Hz; p=0.021).
evidence: Results from combined EEG-fMRI analysis.

claim: No significant correlations of EEG power with fMRI activity were observed in the vmPFC, right DLPFC, or thalamus ROIs.
source: We did not observe significant correlations of EEG power with fMRI activity in the other ROIs.
evidence: Results from combined EEG-fMRI analysis.

claim: Areas exhibiting similar fMRI effects for positive and negative expectations during the anticipation phase are linked to distinct temporal and oscillatory patterns.
source: In summary, the analyses indicated that areas exhibiting similar fMRI effects for positive and negative expectations during the anticipation phase are linked to distinct temporal and oscillatory patterns.
evidence: Summary interpretation of combined EEG-fMRI results.

claim: The left DLPFC and the left anterior insula displayed an early negative correlation between anticipatory activity and EEG power, primarily in the lower frequency range.
source: Notably, the left DLPFC and the left anterior insula displayed an early negative correlation between anticipatory activity and EEG power, primarily in the lower frequency range.
evidence: Summary of combined EEG-fMRI results.

claim: The effects in the bilateral ACC were associated with an increase in gamma oscillations and were observed at later time points during the anticipation phase.
source: Conversely, the subsequent effects in the bilateral ACC were associated with an increase in gamma oscillations and were observed at later time points during the anticipation phase indicating different processes.
evidence: Summary of combined EEG-fMRI results.

claim: The novel within-subjects paradigm was highly effective, as expressed by 47 out of 50 subjects consistently expecting and perceiving the intensity of pain stimuli in line with the cues.
source: Our novel within-subjects paradigm was highly effective, as expressed by 47 out of 50 subjects consistently expecting and perceiving the intensity of pain stimuli in line with the cues that induced positive, negative, or neutral expectations.
evidence: Summary of behavioral results.

claim: The trial-by-trial manipulation of expectations affected self-reports, skin conductance responses, and SIIPS scores.
source: The trial-by-trial manipulation of expectations did not only affect self-reports, but also objective markers such as skin conductance responses and scores of the SIIPS (Woo et al., 2017).
evidence: Summary of multiple outcome measures from the study.

claim: The SIIPS is an indicator of neural activity that tracks differences in pain perception that go beyond pain intensity and is classically affected by placebo and nocebo interventions.
source: The SIIPS is an indicator of neural activity that tracks differences in pain perception that go beyond pain intensity and is classically affected by placebo and nocebo interventions (Botvinik-Nezer et al., 2023; Woo et al., 2017), thus serving as an excellent manipulation check for our paradigm.
evidence: Supported by citations describing the SIIPS.

claim: The SIIPS scores discriminated between positive and negative expectations only during the pain phase and not during the anticipation phase.
source: In line with our expectations, the SIIPS scores discriminated between positive and negative expectations only during the pain phase and not during the anticipation phase.
evidence: Summary of SIIPS analysis results.

claim: The observation of a shift from common to distinct effects in key areas of the DPMS indicates that the activation during the anticipation phase is not just mere pre-activation for later pain modulation.
source: The observation of this pattern in key areas of the DPMS indicates that the activation during the anticipation phase is not just mere pre-activation for later pain modulation, but that preparatory processes that are distinguishable from those that occur during pain perception take place.
evidence: Interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: Preparatory processes that are distinguishable from those that occur during pain perception take place during the anticipation phase.
source: The observation of this pattern in key areas of the DPMS indicates that the activation during the anticipation phase is not just mere pre-activation for later pain modulation, but that preparatory processes that are distinguishable from those that occur during pain perception take place.
evidence: Interpretation of the fMRI results.

claim: Anticipatory processes may include expectation generation and maintenance, while the focus shifts towards the integration of these expectations into the sensory stream and the evaluation of the percept during pain processing.
source: These anticipatory processes may include expectation generation and maintenance, while the focus shifts towards the integration of these expectations into the sensory stream and the evaluation of the percept during pain processing.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the results.

claim: The differentiation during pain is in agreement with studies that found differential effects for positive and negative expectations during pain.
source: Importantly, the spatial resolution of fMRI is limited when it comes to discriminating whether the same pattern of activity is due to identical activation or to activation in different sub-circuits within the same area. Nonetheless, the overlap of areas is an indicator of similar processes involved in a more general preparation process. The observed differentiation during pain is in agreement with the few studies that looked into the neuronal representations of positive and negative expectations and mainly found differential effects, e.g., opposite responses or differentially modulated areas during pain (Benedetti et al., 2020; Crawford et al., 2021; Koyama et al., 2005; Scott et al., 2008).
evidence: Comparison with previous literature supported by citations.

claim: The network of the DPMS around the DLPFC, ACC, and vmPFC appears to play a pivotal role in expectation processes and in the valence-dependent modulation of pain perception.
source: The network of the DPMS around the DLPFC, ACC, and vmPFC appears to play a pivotal role in expectation processes and in the valence-dependent modulation of pain perception.
evidence: Interpretation of the study results.

claim: Following the framework of predictive coding, the DPMS is the network responsible for integrating ascending signals with descending signals in the pain domain.
source: Following the framework of predictive coding, our results would suggest that the DPMS is the network responsible for integrating ascending signals with descending signals in the pain domain and that this process is similar for positive and negative valences during anticipation of pain but differentiates during pain processing.
evidence: Interpretation of results within a theoretical framework.

claim: The integration process in the DPMS is similar for positive and negative valences during anticipation of pain but differentiates during pain processing.
source: Following the framework of predictive coding, our results would suggest that the DPMS is the network responsible for integrating ascending signals with descending signals in the pain domain and that this process is similar for positive and negative valences during anticipation of pain but differentiates during pain processing.
evidence: Interpretation of results within a theoretical framework.

claim: The outstanding role of the DLPFC in placebo effects is well-established and supported by numerous reports of increased DLPFC activity during pain anticipation.
source: The outstanding role of the DLPFC in placebo effects is well-established and supported by numerous reports of increased DLPFC activity during pain anticipation (Watson et al., 2009) as well as during pain processing (Zunhammer et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The DLPFC has been classically associated with top-down-regulation and expectation modulation.
source: This area has been classically associated with top-down-regulation and expectation modulation (Geuter et al., 2017), as when its neuronal excitability is experimentally manipulated, placebo effects can be diminished or enhanced (Egorova et al., 2015; Krummenacher et al., 2010; Tu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to studies.

claim: When DLPFC neuronal excitability is experimentally manipulated, placebo effects can be diminished or enhanced.
source: This area has been classically associated with top-down-regulation and expectation modulation (Geuter et al., 2017), as when its neuronal excitability is experimentally manipulated, placebo effects can be diminished or enhanced (Egorova et al., 2015; Krummenacher et al., 2010; Tu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The early onset of DLPFC activity suggests that the DLPFC plays an important role in the initiation of both positive and negative expectation effects within the DPMS prior to the noxious stimulation.
source: The early onset of DLPFC activity implied by the EEG analysis now suggests that the DLPFC plays an important role in the initiation of both positive and negative expectation effects within the DPMS prior to the noxious stimulation (Frisaldi et al., 2015; Geuter et al., 2017; Rossettini et al., 2023; Wager and Atlas, 2015; Wager et al., 2011).
evidence: Interpretation of EEG-fMRI results supported by citations.

claim: The vmPFC is suggested to integrate the input from the DLPFC and to generate affective meaning in order to maintain expectations.
source: The vmPFC is another important hub within the DPMS which is suggested to integrate the input from the DLPFC and to generate affective meaning in order to maintain expectations (Geuter et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Geuter et al., 2017.

claim: The vmPFC modulates pain perception by directly affecting brainstem systems, e.g., by influencing PAG activity.
source: It further modulates pain perception by directly affecting brainstem systems (Koban et al., 2017), e.g., by influencing PAG activity (Geuter et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: The notion that prefrontal areas exert top-down control over other areas of the DPMS is supported by the earlier timing of DLPFC effects compared to the ACC.
source: The notion that prefrontal areas exert top-down control over other areas of the DPMS is further supported by the earlier timing of DLPFC effects compared to the ACC (Craggs et al., 2014; Watson et al., 2009).
evidence: Interpretation of timing results supported by citations.

claim: The ACC has a direct influence on the activity of the PAG.
source: The ACC also has a direct influence on the activity of the PAG, suggesting that the ACC is another crucial area for pain modulation (Geuter et al., 2017; Livrizzi et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations.

claim: The effect of the bilateral ACC at the transition from the anticipation to the pain phase could be interpreted as a preparatory mechanism for the modulation of incoming sensory information in downstream areas.
source: The effect of the bilateral ACC at the transition from the anticipation to the pain phase as indicated by our combined EEG-fMRI analysis could be interpreted as a preparatory mechanism for the modulation of incoming sensory information in downstream areas, consistent with its supposed role in the DPMS (Geuter et al., 2013; Geuter et al., 2017; Kong et al., 2008).
evidence: Interpretation of results supported by citations.

claim: Reports of ACC activations for both positive and negative expectations during pain anticipation could be understood as a pre-activation of the ACC for pain modulation in either direction.
source: Using this framework, reports of ACC activations for both positive and negative expectations during pain anticipation could be understood as a pre-activation of the ACC for pain modulation in either direction (Rossettini et al., 2023).
evidence: Interpretation of literature supported by citation.

claim: The link between anticipatory activity in the ACC and EEG oscillatory activity was observed in the high gamma band, which is consistent with findings that demonstrate a connection between increased fMRI BOLD signals and a relative shift from lower to higher frequencies.
source: The link between anticipatory activity in the ACC and EEG oscillatory activity was observed in the high gamma band, which is consistent with findings that demonstrate a connection between increased fMRI BOLD signals and a relative shift from lower to higher frequencies (Kilner et al., 2005).
evidence: Interpretation of results supported by citation.

claim: Gamma oscillations have been repeatedly reported in the context of pain and expectations and have been interpreted as reflecting feedforward signals of noxious information.
source: Gamma oscillations have been repeatedly reported in the context of pain and expectations and have been interpreted as reflecting feedforward signals of noxious information (e.g. Ploner et al., 2017; Strube et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: High-frequency oscillations may be instrumental in the transfer of directed expectations from anticipation into pain processing.
source: In combination with our findings, this might imply that high-frequency oscillations may not only signal higher actual or perceived pain intensity during pain processing (Nickel et al., 2022; Ploner et al., 2017; Strube et al., 2021; Tu et al., 2016), but might also be instrumental in the transfer of directed expectations from anticipation into pain processing.
evidence: Speculative interpretation combining current results with previous literature.

claim: A shift from valence-neutral towards valence-dependent processing over time was demonstrated in the anterior insula.
source: Similarly, a shift from valence-neutral towards valence-dependent processing over time was demonstrated in the anterior insula.
evidence: Summary of fMRI results.

claim: The insula is a key brain region involved in the network responsible for pain processing.
source: The insula is a key brain region involved in the network responsible for pain processing (e.g. Atlas and Wager, 2014; Kober et al., 2008) but is also part of several non-pain-related networks and works as a multimodal network hub (Horing and Büchel, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Results of the fMRI-informed EEG analysis indicated early effects in the anticipatory period consistent with an early role of the anterior insula in expectation generation and initiation.
source: Results of the fMRI-informed EEG analysis indicated early effects in the anticipatory period consistent with an early role of the anterior insula in expectation generation and initiation.
evidence: Interpretation of combined EEG-fMRI results.

claim: Due to the multimodal nature of the insula, multiple networks may interact to integrate relevant information from different domains into an expectancy signal in the anterior insula.
source: Due to the multimodal nature of the insula, it may be speculated that multiple networks interact to integrate relevant information from different domains (e.g. from the visual cue and interoceptive information) into an expectancy signal in the anterior insula.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on known properties of the insula.

claim: The anterior insula may encode the expected threat level and salience of subsequent pain stimuli, leading to an anticipatory activation prior to the actual perceptual modulation.
source: Due to its connections and function within the salience network, this may involve encoding the expected threat level and salience of subsequent pain stimuli, leading to an anticipatory activation prior to the actual perceptual modulation (Taesler and Rose, 2016; Wiech et al., 2010).
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citations.

claim: During pain perception, the anterior insula may be more engaged in a network responsible for stimulus processing and evaluating actual salience and prediction errors in this perceptual process.
source: During pain perception, the anterior insula may then be more engaged in a network responsible for stimulus processing and evaluating actual salience and prediction errors in this perceptual process (Horing and Büchel, 2022), which may imply that the insula is involved in multiple tasks over time.
evidence: Speculative interpretation supported by citation.

claim: The activation of the angular gyrus during pain processing and pain anticipation could be understood as an indicator for processes related to the formation and integration of directed expectations.
source: Similar to the anterior insula, the activation of the angular gyrus during pain processing and pain anticipation could be understood as an indicator for processes related to the formation and integration of directed expectations.
evidence: Interpretation of fMRI results.

claim: The angular gyrus has been connected to expectation-related pain modulation only a few times.
source: The angular gyrus has been connected to expectation-related pain modulation only a few times (e.g. Atlas and Wager, 2014; Tu et al., 2019) but its involvement is prominent in our results.
evidence: Statement about limited previous literature supported by citations.

claim: Based on its presumed function in maintaining recollected multimodal representations, the angular gyrus may be engaged in transforming sensory information from the visual cues into expectancy signals.
source: Based on its presumed function in maintaining recollected multimodal representations (Jablonowski and Rose, 2022; Vilberg and Rugg, 2012), the angular gyrus may be engaged in transforming sensory information from the visual cues into expectancy signals that can be processed by e.g., the DPMS and salience network.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on known functions supported by citations.

claim: The expectation manipulation in this study falls in line with a manipulation of treatment expectancies, a typical method of expectation manipulation in placebo paradigms.
source: While this may give rise to questions regarding the comparability of our study to previous paradigms and the manner in which our control condition was employed, we would argue that our expectation manipulation falls in line with a manipulation of treatment expectancies, a typical method of expectation manipulation in placebo paradigms (see Atlas and Wager, 2014).
evidence: Justification of methodology supported by citation.

claim: The study's expectation manipulation is comparable to previous studies on placebo and nocebo effects.
source: Accordingly, it is comparable to previous studies on placebo and nocebo effects.
evidence: Inference about comparability to previous research.

claim: The study's manipulation is comparable to studies utilizing sham TENS-devices that are supposedly altering peripheral pain transmission.
source: This is, in a broader sense, comparable to studies utilizing sham TENS-devices that are supposedly altering peripheral pain transmission (Skvortsova et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison to other methodologies supported by citation.

claim: Implementing a proper control condition in expectation modulation paradigms is an inherently difficult task as forming expectations about our environment is a natural process.
source: Moreover, implementing a proper control condition in expectation modulation paradigms is an inherently difficult task as forming expectations about our environment is a natural process.
evidence: Statement about methodological challenges based on general knowledge.

claim: Participants most likely did form expectations of medium pain intensities in the control condition over the course of the experiment.
source: Therefore, we recognize that participants most likely did form expectations of medium pain intensities in the control condition over the course of the experiment.
evidence: Inference about participant behavior.

claim: In previous research on placebo and nocebo effects, participants typically rated control stimuli in between placebo and nocebo conditions.
source: This is in line with previous research on placebo and nocebo effects, in which participants also typically rated control stimuli in between placebo and nocebo conditions (Bingel et al., 2011; Colloca et al., 2010; Shih et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The crucial difference between the control condition and the placebo/nocebo conditions is that there was no alteration of perception due to previous experiences or verbal information and no shift of perception from the actual stimulus intensity towards any direction in the control condition.
source: Independently of whether participants build up an expectation of 'medium' intensities in the control condition, which caused them to perceive stimuli in line with this, or if they simply perceived the stimuli as they were (of medium intensity) with limited effects of expectations, the crucial difference to the placebo and nocebo conditions is that there was no alteration of perception due to previous experiences or verbal information and no shift of perception from the actual stimulus intensity towards any direction in the control condition.
evidence: Explanation of the control condition rationale.

claim: The study was able to identify the effects of directed expectations by comparing positive and negative expectations to neutral expectations as a baseline.
source: Thus, we were able to identify the effects of directed expectations by comparing positive and negative expectations to neutral expectations as a baseline.
evidence: Description of the analytical approach.

claim: Ratings varied within conditions and the amount of variation was comparable between nocebo and control.
source: Our analysis of within-condition variability further showed that ratings indeed varied within conditions and that the amount of variation was comparable between nocebo and control.
evidence: Summary of variability analysis results.

claim: Over time, expectations were dynamically updated in all three conditions.
source: Over time, expectations were dynamically updated in all three conditions, speaking against alternative explanations of the rating differences between conditions such as a regression to the mean of ratings in the control condition.
evidence: Summary of temporal analysis results.

claim: Understanding the processing of expectations requires an examination of its temporal and spatial dynamics from anticipation to pain processing, while comparing positive and negative valences to each other and to a control condition.
source: Based on the present results, understanding the processing of expectations requires an examination of its temporal and spatial dynamics from anticipation to pain processing, while comparing positive and negative valences to each other and to a control condition.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: The study found largely comparable activation for positive and negative expectations during the anticipation phase, including regions outside of those classically observed in pain processing and modulation.
source: We found largely comparable activation for positive and negative expectations during the anticipation phase, including regions outside of those classically observed in pain processing and modulation.
evidence: Summary of main findings.

claim: Based on the observed temporal profiles, the DLPFC and anterior insula may be related to the top-down initiation and generation of expectations.
source: Based on the observed temporal profiles, the DLPFC and anterior insula may be related to the top-down initiation and generation of expectations, while the ACC is activated in close proximity to pain onset as a direct link to pain modulation.
evidence: Interpretation of temporal results.

claim: The ACC is activated in close proximity to pain onset as a direct link to pain modulation.
source: Based on the observed temporal profiles, the DLPFC and anterior insula may be related to the top-down initiation and generation of expectations, while the ACC is activated in close proximity to pain onset as a direct link to pain modulation.
evidence: Interpretation of temporal results.

claim: During the pain phase, the focus shifts from expectation generation and maintenance towards pain modulation in either positive or negative direction.
source: During the pain phase, the focus shifts from expectation generation and maintenance towards pain modulation in either positive or negative direction, leading to distinct effects of positive and negative expectations in many areas that initially encoded expectations independently of their valence.
evidence: Interpretation of the temporal dynamics of results.

claim: Pain perception was recently described as a complex process of interactions among multiple brain systems that are reconfigured over time.
source: It is not surprising that expectations are not a static process but involve different time-dependent components, as pain perception was also recently described as a complex process of interactions among multiple brain systems that are reconfigured over time (Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2022.

claim: Expectation generation, integration, and pain perception all appear to be dynamic processes, with both common and distinct routes for positive and negative expectations, depending on the time point of examination.
source: Expectation generation, integration, and pain perception all appear to be dynamic processes, with both common and distinct routes for positive and negative expectations, depending on the time point of examination.
evidence: Overall conclusion from the study results.
